Environment: provider=alibaba stage=prod mode=auto page=none
secretsmanager service or LocalStack, which one i choose for production?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md#secret-managers-on-premises]
Keep API keys, database passwords and certificates in a secret manager instead of files, and read them from handlers with **one call that works on every provider**: No extra library: the calls are part of the pskit runtime (Python standard library, Node.js built-ins). Values are cached for 60 seconds per function instance.

For production, pick `secretsmanager` (or OpenBao); LocalStack is meant for development and tests.

| Service | API | Keeps data | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `secretsmanager` / `secretsmanager-node` | AWS Secrets Manager, every request checked with SigV4 | one JSON file in a volume, `.tar.gz` backups | real use |
| OpenBao (`openbao`) | HashiCorp Vault, KV v2 | file storage in a volume, unsealed on start | real use |
| LocalStack (`localstack`) | Secrets Manager + SSM Parameter Store | with `PERSISTENCE=1` | development and tests |

pskit's own server checks every request's signature, which LocalStack does not.

Environment: provider=onprem stage=staging mode=auto page=Setup
What is `--advertise` for on `cluster join`? Writing docs for it.

`--advertise IP` sets the address the server announces to the rest of the cluster. Use it when a server has more than one address and the others must reach it on a specific one. The same flag exists on `pskit cluster create` for the master:

```
pskit cluster join staging app-2 --advertise 198.51.100.12
```

Environment: provider=onprem stage=prod mode=auto page=Setup
Run locally on Test: does the function need to be on the server first? Where I come from you deploy before you can test anything.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#test-functions]
1. Pick the function and the event: one of its triggers (HTTP, schedule, queue, storage, topic) or **Direct invoke**. 2. Edit the payload. It starts from a sample for that trigger type (a storage sample matches the trigger's prefix and suffix; a schedule uses its own `input`). **Save event** keeps named payloads per function in `.pskit/studio/test-events.json`, like test events in the Lambda console. 3. **Run locally** runs the handler on this machine with a synthetic event (`pskit invoke`): no cloud, no deploy. **Send to <provider>/<stage>** fires the real trigger of the deployed function (`pskit trigger`): a queue message, an uploaded object, a topic message, an HTTP request or an invocation. Turn on *Show the function's logs* to watch it.

No. Run locally runs the handler on this machine with a synthetic event (`pskit invoke`): no deploy and nothing remote. Only Send needs the deployed function.

When the function is deployed, section "3. Run it" also shows a Server picker, so you choose which server the Send goes to.


Environment: provider=alibaba stage=dev mode=ask page=Code
order-events topic resource on Tencent. YAML?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/tencent/topic.md#tencent-cloud-tdmq-for-cmq-topic-type-topic]
> **No topic trigger on Tencent Cloud.** pskit's Tencent provider has no `topic` event: `pskit validate` rejects > `- topic: ...` there. Declare the topic as an external resource and publish with the Tencent Cloud SDK. Subscribers > (queues, HTTP endpoints) are configured on the topic in the console.

External topic, keys by variable name:

```yaml
provider:
  name: tencent
  environment:
    TDMQ_SECRET_ID: ${env:TDMQ_SECRET_ID}
    TDMQ_SECRET_KEY: ${env:TDMQ_SECRET_KEY}

resources:
  order-events:
    type: topic
    external: true
    name: order-events
    connection:
      region: ap-guangzhou
      secret_id_env: TDMQ_SECRET_ID
      secret_key_env: TDMQ_SECRET_KEY
```

No `topic` event on any function.

my functions get lot of traffic. better master serve or not serve?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cluster.md#load-balancer-one-url-for-the-whole-cluster-optional]
Add one more saved server **outside** the cluster as its load balancer. pskit runs OpenResty (nginx) there in Docker (container `pskit-lb`, host network) and spreads each deployment's HTTP over the cluster's servers with the algorithm you pick (`--algorithm`: round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin, IP hash, least connections (the default) or least time; `--weight edge1=3` per server; see [load balancers](load-balancers.md#the-six-algorithms)). It works the same way for all three orchestrators. To share one load balancer between clusters and projects by path instead (`http://lb/<service>/`), attach a named one: `pskit lb attach edge --cluster prod` ([load balancers](load-balancers.md)).

With heavy traffic, consider turning it off. When the master serves, it uses its spare CPU, but that traffic competes with the control plane, schedules, queues and data that live on the master. With it off, the master is a backup and only gets requests while every other server is down.

**In the terminal**

```
pskit cluster set prod --no-master-serves
```

On Swarm and k3s, run `pskit deploy` after that so the web replicas leave the master.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/load-balancers.md#create-one-and-put-projects-on-it]
A project names it in `pskit.yml`; every `pskit deploy` updates its route and `pskit remove` drops it: The path prefix is removed before the request reaches your functions (`/shop/orders` arrives as `/orders`) and sent in `X-Forwarded-Prefix: /shop`. `/shop` redirects to `/shop/`. A **cluster** can be attached instead; every deployment on it gets `/<service>/` (or `/<service>-<stage>/` when two stages of a service share the cluster), kept up to date on deploy, remove, join and leave: A project's own `balancer` setting wins over the cluster's route for that deployment. A project whose [placement groups](placement.md) run on several attached clusters gets one route, `/<service>/`, to the servers of all of them; each server passes another group's routes on to it.

All four that change routes: deploy, remove, join and leave. After each one the route for every deployment on the cluster (`/<service>/`, or `/<service>-<stage>/` for two stages) must match the cluster's current servers. Add a case where the project has its own `balancer` setting, which must win over the cluster's route.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/client.md#when-connections-time-out]
`TimeoutError` / `ConnectTimeoutError` / `ECONNREFUSED` from a script almost always mean a firewall: the program can't open a TCP connection to that port. The service is usually fine (`pskit resources onprem status <key>`). Generated direct-client examples use short connect timeouts (about 5 s), so a closed port fails quickly with this explanation in mind instead of hanging. The studio flags it too: *On-prem services → Details* shows when this machine cannot reach a service, and *Call from code* checks the host.

**In studio**

1. Open `Resources > On-prem services`.
2. Open the Details of the Redis service. It shows when this machine cannot reach the service.

When it does, the usual cause is a firewall on the server's port, and `pskit resources onprem tunnel redis` gets you in over SSH.

messages.content:
[docs/load-balancers.md#create-one-and-put-projects-on-it]
A project names it in `pskit.yml`; every `pskit deploy` updates its route and `pskit remove` drops it: The path prefix is removed before the request reaches your functions (`/shop/orders` arrives as `/orders`) and sent in `X-Forwarded-Prefix: /shop`. `/shop` redirects to `/shop/`. A **cluster** can be attached instead; every deployment on it gets `/<service>/` (or `/<service>-<stage>/` when two stages of a service share the cluster), kept up to date on deploy, remove, join and leave: A project's own `balancer` setting wins over the cluster's route for that deployment. A project whose [placement groups](placement.md) run on several attached clusters gets one route, `/<service>/`, to the servers of all of them; each server passes another group's routes on to it.
No. `pskit remove` drops the project's route from the balancer, and the next `pskit deploy` writes it again, since every deploy updates that route.
We test dev and staging of shop on the same attached cluster. Same path for both?
No, when two stages of a service share the cluster each gets `/<service>-<stage>/`, so you would call `/shop-dev/` and `/shop-staging/`. With a single stage it is just `/shop/`.

least_time and round_robin — what's the real difference between them? I'm new to load balancers.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/load-balancers.md#the-six-algorithms]
**Static** algorithms follow a fixed rule; **dynamic** ones measure live load per request. Open-source nginx has no sticky cookie or least time (both are NGINX Plus), so pskit builds them: sticky hashes a cookie that holds the first request's id (`hash ... consistent`), and least time runs `balancer_by_lua` with a moving average of each server's response header time. A server that fails is retried on the next one and rests for 10 s.

`round_robin` is a **static** algorithm: it follows a fixed rule and sends each request to the next server in turn. `least_time` is **dynamic**: it measures live load per request, keeping a moving average of each server's response header time and picking the faster one.
Plain nginx can do least_time?
Not open-source nginx; least time is an NGINX Plus feature. pskit builds it itself by running `balancer_by_lua` with that moving average, so you get it without Plus.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cluster.md#how-the-functions-run-in-a-cluster]
* **web** replicas serve your HTTP routes and `invoke()` calls. Adding replicas or servers adds HTTP capacity. * The **main** replica runs on the master with the data volume. It owns everything stateful: schedules run once, not once per replica; built-in queues, topics and buckets live in one place; workflow executions are recorded there; queue, storage and topic triggers run there. * A web replica hands those to main. `submit_queue()`, `put_object()`, workflow starts and `/__pskit/*` admin calls are forwarded to it. Each web replica listens on its own server's port, one replica per server, and the main replica listens on the master's port. Nomad does not spread HTTP across the servers for you.

So a request to app-2 is answered by app-2's web replica, and a request to the master by main. For one URL that spreads requests, let pskit run a load balancer on one more server, or put your own nginx, HAProxy or Traefik in front.

```yaml
resources:

functions:

    handler: app.handlers.on_invoice
    events:

```

```bash
pskit validate
```

Environment: provider=onprem stage=staging mode=auto page=Test
My test script wants to call the on-prem host. Does the pskit client need extra pip packages?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/architecture.md#deploy-pipeline]
- **Terraform JSON, not HCL.** The generator builds Python dicts, so there's no quoting or templating to get wrong. User strings are escaped (`${` → `$${`) unless written as `${tf:...}`. - **Reproducible artifacts.** The zip is byte-identical for identical inputs. Unchanged code means an unchanged hash and no redeploy. - **One directory per provider and stage.** Each has its own Terraform workspace and state, so `aws-dev` and `gcp-prod` never interfere. - **Every provider emits a `pskit` output** with the shape `{functions: {name: {id, arn?, url?, base_url?, console?}}, workflows: {...}, endpoint}`. `pskit info` and the dashboard use only this output, which keeps them provider-agnostic.

No extra packages: `client.py` uses only the standard library. Point the script at the host and run it.

**In the terminal**

1. Run your script from a machine that can reach the host, for example:

```
python tests/call_host.py
```

pskit can **create** the queue, stream, bucket, database or cache your on-premises functions use, then add it to `pskit.yml` as a resource and, for queues, streams and buckets, as a trigger. Environment: provider=onprem stage=staging mode=auto page=Cluster
The Cluster page marks one replica as main. Why is it always on the master?

function.name: search_docs
function.arguments: {"query": "main replica runs on the master data volume"}

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cluster.md#how-the-functions-run-in-a-cluster]
* **web** replicas serve your HTTP routes and `invoke()` calls. Adding replicas or servers adds HTTP capacity. * The **main** replica runs on the master with the data volume. It owns everything stateful: schedules run once, not once per replica; built-in queues, topics and buckets live in one place; workflow executions are recorded there; queue, storage and topic triggers run there. * A web replica hands those to main. `submit_queue()`, `put_object()`, workflow starts and `/__pskit/*` admin calls are forwarded to it. Its log lines and invocation counts are sent to main every second, tagged with `replica`, so `pskit logs`, the studio's **Logs** view and `/__pskit/stats` show the whole cluster. * Resources with a driver (Redis, SQS, S3, MinIO, ...) are used directly by every replica, as on one server.

Because the master holds the data volume, and main owns everything stateful:

- schedules, run once
- built-in queues, topics and buckets
- workflow execution records
- queue, storage and topic triggers

Keeping all of that on one machine is what makes a schedule fire once and a queue keep one copy of each message.

Environment: provider=oracle stage=staging mode=ask page=Code
psycopg in my handler on the Code page. Should I open a new connection on every call?

Better not. The on-prem host is a long-running process, so a module-level pool is created once and reused across invocations.

**In code**

`requirements.txt`:

```text
psycopg[binary]
psycopg_pool
```

```python
from psycopg_pool import ConnectionPool
from py_serverless_kit import resource

_pool = None


def _get_pool(ctx):
    global _pool
    if _pool is None:
        db = resource("orders-db")
        conninfo = "host={} port={} dbname={} user={} password={}".format(
            db["host"], db["port"], db["database"], db["user"], ctx.env[db["password_env"]]
        )
        _pool = ConnectionPool(conninfo)
    return _pool


def api(event, ctx):
    with _get_pool(ctx).connection() as conn:
        count = conn.execute("select count(*) from orders").fetchone()[0]
    return {"orders": count}
```

Dependencies are installed on premises when you deploy.

resources list and resources delete, how they work together?

|---|---|

| Delete one or more by address | `pskit resources delete <address> -s dev` |
| Delete everything kept by remove | `pskit resources delete --all-kept -s dev` |

Environment: provider=cloudflare stage=dev mode=auto page=Workflows
Workflow orchestrator on cloudflare dev got a public route I didn't ask for. Intended?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/troubleshooting.md#security-notes]
- 500 responses never include exception details unless `PSKIT_DEBUG` is set. - `.env`, Terraform state and `pskit*.yml` are excluded from bundles. `.pskit/` is git-ignored. - `auth: none` routes are public. Embedded workflow orchestrators get a public `POST /workflows/<name>` route unless you set `options.http: false`. - `resources:` connection values are function environment variables: they land in Terraform state and, on premises, in `pskit_host.json`. Pass the *name* of a secret variable instead of the secret ([resources.md](resources.md#secrets)). - On premises, set `admin_token` when the host binds beyond loopback: it guards `/__pskit/*` (queues, invoke, workflows, executions, logs, stats). `pskit dashboard --serve` binds loopback and never sends that token to the browser. - Created AWS buckets block public access. Prefer a least-privilege `iam.statements` over `"*"` resources. - Keep secrets out of YAML: use `${env:...}` in CI or a secret manager via `${tf:...}`. - Report vulnerabilities privately (see `SECURITY.md` in the repository root).

Intended. Embedded workflow orchestrators get a public `POST /workflows/<name>` route unless you set `options.http: false`.

**In code**

```yaml
workflows:
  nightly-sync:
    options:
      http: false
```

**In the terminal**

1. Confirm the config:

```bash
pskit validate -p cloudflare -s dev
```

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/load-balancers.md#create-one-and-put-projects-on-it]
A project names it in `pskit.yml`; every `pskit deploy` updates its route and `pskit remove` drops it: The path prefix is removed before the request reaches your functions (`/shop/orders` arrives as `/orders`) and sent in `X-Forwarded-Prefix: /shop`. `/shop` redirects to `/shop/`. A **cluster** can be attached instead; every deployment on it gets `/<service>/` (or `/<service>-<stage>/` when two stages of a service share the cluster), kept up to date on deploy, remove, join and leave: A project's own `balancer` setting wins over the cluster's route for that deployment. A project whose [placement groups](placement.md) run on several attached clusters gets one route, `/<service>/`, to the servers of all of them; each server passes another group's routes on to it.
`/orders`. The path prefix is removed before the request reaches your functions, and the prefix is sent in the `X-Forwarded-Prefix: /shop` header.
And someone opens /shop with no slash?

`/shop` redirects to `/shop/`.

**In studio**

1. Open `Load balancers > + Create load balancer` if you do not have `edge` yet.

**In the terminal**

```
pskit lb create edge --server app-1 --port 80
```

Environment: provider=onprem stage=prod mode=ask page=Overview
`pskit-<service>-<stage>` on a cluster = which workloads?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cluster.md#how-the-functions-run-in-a-cluster]
* **web** replicas serve your HTTP routes and `invoke()` calls. Adding replicas or servers adds HTTP capacity. * The **main** replica runs on the master with the data volume. It owns everything stateful: schedules run once, not once per replica; built-in queues, topics and buckets live in one place; workflow executions are recorded there; queue, storage and topic triggers run there. * A web replica hands those to main. `submit_queue()`, `put_object()`, workflow starts and `/__pskit/*` admin calls are forwarded to it. Its log lines and invocation counts are sent to main every second, tagged with `replica`, so `pskit logs`, the studio's **Logs** view and `/__pskit/stats` show the whole cluster. * Resources with a driver (Redis, SQS, S3, MinIO, ...) are used directly by every replica, as on one server.

Two, same function host image:

| Workload | Count | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| web | N, spread over servers | HTTP routes, `invoke()` |
| main | 1, on the master with the data volume | schedules, built-in queues / topics / buckets, workflow executions, queue / storage / topic triggers |

Environment: provider=ibm stage=staging mode=auto page=Logs
RabbitMQ exchange, publish from on-prem handler. Pattern?

Declare the broker as a `custom` resource and publish with its client library; RabbitMQ exchanges are not a topic driver.

**In code**

```yaml
resources:
  rabbit:
    type: custom
    external: true
    connection:
      host: mq.example.com
      port: 5672
      user: deploy
      password_env: RABBIT_PASSWORD
```

```python
import pika
from py_serverless_kit import resource


def api(event, ctx):
    mq = resource("rabbit")
    creds = pika.PlainCredentials(mq["user"], ctx.env[mq["password_env"]])
    params = pika.ConnectionParameters(host=mq["host"], port=int(mq["port"]), credentials=creds)
    with pika.BlockingConnection(params) as conn:
        conn.channel().basic_publish(exchange="orders", routing_key="paid", body=b"order paid")
    return {"published": True}
```

Add `pika` to `requirements.txt`. To consume from an exchange instead, bind a queue and use a custom queue driver.

Environment: provider=onprem stage=staging mode=ask page=Resources
pskit_host.json shows my redis password in plain text on db-1. How do I stop that?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/troubleshooting.md#security-notes]
- 500 responses never include exception details unless `PSKIT_DEBUG` is set. - `.env`, Terraform state and `pskit*.yml` are excluded from bundles. `.pskit/` is git-ignored. - `auth: none` routes are public. Embedded workflow orchestrators get a public `POST /workflows/<name>` route unless you set `options.http: false`. - `resources:` connection values are function environment variables: they land in Terraform state and, on premises, in `pskit_host.json`. Pass the *name* of a secret variable instead of the secret ([resources.md](resources.md#secrets)). - On premises, set `admin_token` when the host binds beyond loopback: it guards `/__pskit/*` (queues, invoke, workflows, executions, logs, stats). `pskit dashboard --serve` binds loopback and never sends that token to the browser. - Created AWS buckets block public access. Prefer a least-privilege `iam.statements` over `"*"` resources. - Keep secrets out of YAML: use `${env:...}` in CI or a secret manager via `${tf:...}`. - Report vulnerabilities privately (see `SECURITY.md` in the repository root).

`resources:` connection values become function environment variables, and on premises they're written into `pskit_host.json`. Pass the *name* of a secret variable instead of the secret, so only that name lands in the file.

**In code**

```yaml
resources:
  cache:
    type: cache
    external: true
    connection:
      host: 192.0.2.20
      port: 6379
      password_env: CACHE_PASSWORD
```

**In the terminal**

1. Check the config:

```bash
pskit validate -s staging
```

2. Redeploy so `pskit_host.json` is rewritten:

```bash
pskit deploy -s staging
```

If the host binds beyond loopback, also set `admin_token`, because it guards `/__pskit/*`.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/architecture.md#deploy-pipeline]
- **Terraform JSON, not HCL.** The generator builds Python dicts, so there's no quoting or templating to get wrong. User strings are escaped (`${` → `$${`) unless written as `${tf:...}`. - **Reproducible artifacts.** The zip is byte-identical for identical inputs. Unchanged code means an unchanged hash and no redeploy. - **One directory per provider and stage.** Each has its own Terraform workspace and state, so `aws-dev` and `gcp-prod` never interfere. - **Every provider emits a `pskit` output** with the shape `{functions: {name: {id, arn?, url?, base_url?, console?}}, workflows: {...}, endpoint}`. `pskit info` and the dashboard use only this output, which keeps them provider-agnostic.

Under `.pskit/digitalocean-dev/`: one directory per provider and stage, each with its own Terraform workspace and state. It is Terraform JSON built from Python dicts, not HCL.

**In the terminal**

1. Validate first, so the schema and provider checks run before you read the file:

```
pskit validate -s dev
```

2. Then open `.pskit/digitalocean-dev/main.tf.json`.

Before the prod deploy: our Kinesis stream is declared as `type: custom`. Will pskit add IAM for it, or do we hit AccessDenied after release?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/aws/custom.md#other-aws-services-type-custom]
`custom` is for any service that isn't a bucket, queue, topic, database or cache: DynamoDB, Secrets Manager, Kinesis, EventBridge, Bedrock, a third-party API. pskit only passes its details to your functions (`external: true` is required). pskit grants **no IAM permissions** for `custom` resources: add them under `provider.iam.statements`. Use `${tf:...}` only for resources you also define in `provider.terraform.extra`; for console-created ones, paste the ARN.

You will hit AccessDenied unless you add the permissions yourself. pskit grants no IAM permissions for `custom` resources; it only passes the resource's details to your functions, and `external: true` is required.

What to do before the release:

1. Add a statement under `provider.iam.statements` with the stream actions your handler calls, scoped to the stream ARN.
2. Paste the console ARN in the resource's `connection`; `${tf:...}` is only for resources you also define in `provider.terraform.extra`.

**In the terminal**

1. Validate and check what the function receives before you deploy:

```bash
pskit validate
pskit resources send --list
```

messages.name: search_docs

Per group: one of `server`, `cluster` or `local: true` (the default group may leave it out and use `options.deploy` / `--server` as before), `functions`, and optionally `port` (needed when two groups share a server) and `advertise` (the URL the other groups call, when the server's own address is not reachable).

Bucket naming + endpoint for COS, used to S3's. Differences?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/ibm/storage.md#ibm-cloud-object-storage-bucket-type-storage]
Read and write objects in a Cloud Object Storage (COS) bucket from a handler. **Not supported on IBM Cloud:** `storage` triggers (a function that runs when an object is uploaded). Watch the bucket from the [on-premises host](../../resources.md#storage-drivers) with `driver: ibm_cos` instead, or have the uploader call the function's URL.

Names follow similar rules: unique, 3-63 lowercase letters, digits, dots and dashes. The difference is the endpoint: with COS you always pass one, from bucket → **Configuration** → **Endpoints** → *Public*, for example `s3.us-south.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud`. Region is under **Configuration** → *Location*.

**In code**

```yaml
resources:
  invoices:
    type: storage
```

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/troubleshooting.md#installation-and-tooling]
**`pip install failed while vendoring dependencies`** : For vendoring providers (aws, alibaba, ibm, digitalocean, tencent, huawei), pskit downloads **Linux** wheels (`manylinux2014_<arch>`, `--only-binary=:all:`) for the target Python version. Error: `pip install failed while vendoring dependencies`. pskit pulls `manylinux2014_<arch>` wheels with `--only-binary=:all:` for the target Python, and that grpcio version has none.

- Pin a grpcio version that publishes manylinux wheels.
- Add pip flags via `package.pip_args`.
- Isolate the rest of the build with `pskit package --skip-deps`.

**In the terminal**

1. Build without dependencies to confirm the rest is fine:

```bash
pskit package -s prod --skip-deps
```

2. After pinning grpcio, build the full bundle with the pip output visible:

```bash
pskit package -s prod -v
```

HTTP API with a key from a secret binding, wiring?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/cloudflare/custom.md#other-cloudflare-services-and-apis-type-custom]
`custom` covers anything else a Worker talks to: a secret, Workers AI, Vectorize, another Worker, or any HTTP API. pskit only passes `connection` values to handlers (`external: true` is required). Either bind the service through `functions.<fn>.options.bindings` or call its HTTP API. Python Workers can't install packages, so use bindings or `from js import fetch` rather than SDKs.

Keep the key in a `secret_text` binding filled from `${env:...}`, and tell the handler the binding name through `connection`.

**In code**

```yaml
resources:
  payments:
    type: custom
    external: true
    connection:
      base_url: https://api.payments.example.com/v1
      secret_binding: PAYMENTS_KEY

functions:
  checkout:
    handler: app.handlers.checkout
    options:
      bindings:
        - {type: secret_text, name: PAYMENTS_KEY, text: "${env:PAYMENTS_KEY}"}
```

The handler reads the binding named in `secret_binding` and calls `base_url` with `from js import fetch`.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#security]
- It binds to `127.0.0.1` by default. - Every API call needs the session token from the printed URL. Anyone who has that URL has full access, so don't share it. A new token is generated each time studio starts. - Requests with a foreign `Host` header (DNS rebinding) or a cross-site `Origin` are refused, and bodies are capped at 2 MiB. - The file editor only reaches files inside the project. It never touches `.pskit/`, `.git/`, `.venv/`, `node_modules/` or `__pycache__`, and refuses binary files or files over 1 MiB. - Deploy commands run as `python -m py_serverless_kit ...` with explicit arguments, never through a shell.
Not a bug. The editor never touches `__pycache__` or `node_modules/`, and it also skips `.pskit/`, `.git/` and `.venv/`.

[docs/architecture.md#deploy-pipeline]
- **Terraform JSON, not HCL.** The generator builds Python dicts, so there's no quoting or templating to get wrong. User strings are escaped (`${` → `$${`) unless written as `${tf:...}`. - **Reproducible artifacts.** The zip is byte-identical for identical inputs. Environment: provider=oracle stage=staging mode=ask page=YAML
"certificate verify failed" with IBM Databases for Redis from my function. Redis lib is new for me.

IBM's Redis always uses TLS (`rediss://`) with the instance's own self-signed CA, so the client must be given that CA certificate through `ssl_ca_certs`.

**In code**

1. Copy the certificate from **Endpoints** → *TLS certificate* (base64) into the `CACHE_CA_B64` setting, and reference it from pskit.yml:

```yaml
provider:
  name: ibm
  environment:
    CACHE_CA_B64: ${env:CACHE_CA_B64}
    CACHE_PASSWORD: ${env:CACHE_PASSWORD}
resources:
  cache:
    type: cache
    external: true
    connection:
      host: xxxx.databases.appdomain.cloud
      port: 30123
```

2. Write it to a file and pass it to the client:

```python
import base64
import os

import redis
from py_serverless_kit import resource


def main(event, context):
    c = resource("cache")
    ca_path = "/tmp/redis-ca.pem"
    with open(ca_path, "wb") as fh:
        fh.write(base64.b64decode(os.environ["CACHE_CA_B64"]))
    client = redis.Redis(
        host=c["host"],
        port=int(c["port"]),
        username="admin",
        password=os.environ["CACHE_PASSWORD"],
        ssl=True,
        ssl_ca_certs=ca_path,
    )
    return {"pong": client.ping()}
```

from js import fetch is the only way out of a Python Worker? Need to publish to an SNS-style topic in another cloud, and boto3 is what the old code used.

Yes. There are no SDKs on Python Workers, so the handler calls the other cloud's HTTP API with `fetch` from `js`.

**In code**

```python
import json

from js import Object, fetch
from pyodide.ffi import to_js
from py_serverless_kit import resource


async def api(event, ctx):
    topic = resource("order-events")
    init = {"method": "POST", "body": json.dumps(event.http.json()),
            "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer " + ctx.raw.EVENTS_TOKEN,
                        "Content-Type": "application/json"}}
    resp = await fetch(topic["publish_url"], to_js(init, dict_converter=Object.fromEntries))
    return {"status": resp.status}
```

The topic itself is declared `type: topic`, `external: true` with a `publish_url` in `connection`, and the token comes from a `secret_text` binding.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/aws/cache.md#amazon-elasticache-memorydb-type-cache]
Redis OSS or Valkey on ElastiCache (serverless or node-based) or MemoryDB. pskit never creates caches: declare them with `external: true`. ElastiCache and MemoryDB are **only reachable from inside their VPC**. pskit deploys Lambda functions outside any VPC unless you set `functions.<fn>.options.vpc_config`, so a function that uses the cache needs it (see step 3).

**In studio**

2. Open `Resources > How to use` for the variables and a snippet for your handler.

**In the terminal**

1. Validate, then list what the functions will receive:

```bash
pskit validate
pskit resources send --list
```

Remember the function also needs `options.vpc_config`, because the cache is reachable only from inside its VPC.

messages.name: search_docs

Add one more saved server **outside** the cluster as its load balancer. pskit runs OpenResty (nginx) there in Docker (container `pskit-lb`, host network) and spreads each deployment's HTTP over the cluster's servers with the algorithm you pick (`--algorithm`: round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin, IP hash, least connections (the default) or least time; `--weight edge1=3` per server; see [load balancers](load-balancers.md#the-six-algorithms)). No. The load balancer spreads each deployment's HTTP over the cluster's servers. A schedule is not an HTTP request from users, so the load balancer does not handle it.

`--delete-data` plus `--uninstall` for cluster billing, what data goes away, and what stays?

Main-replica data is removed only with both flags. `--uninstall` stops the deployments and takes off the load balancer, the agents and the orchestrator. `--delete-data` then deletes the main replicas' data on the master. Saved servers stay.

**In the terminal**


Environment: provider=alibaba stage=dev mode=ask page=Functions
redis client for type: cache, ssl and password handling in handler?

**In code**

1. Add `redis` to `requirements.txt`.
2. Build the client once and reuse it across warm invocations. Connection booleans arrive as strings, so compare `ssl` with `"true"`, and only pass a password when `password_env` is set:

```python
import redis
from py_serverless_kit import resource

_client = None


def api(event, ctx):
    global _client
    if _client is None:
        c = resource("cache")
        password_env = c.get("password_env")
        password = ctx.env[password_env] if password_env else None
        _client = redis.Redis(host=c["host"], port=int(c["port"]), ssl=c.get("ssl") == "true", password=password)
    return {"hits": _client.incr("hits")}
```

For a cluster-mode endpoint use `redis.cluster.RedisCluster` instead.

@ in the Cloudflare Name field, when would I use that for the mail records?

function.name: search_docs
function.arguments: {"query": "DNS record name at sign root domain"}

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/smtp/README.md#dns-records-at-your-domain-provider]
- Most providers want only the part before your root domain in *Name*: `mail.inbound` and `inbound` for `example.com`, or `@` for the root domain itself. `10` is the MX priority; some providers have a separate field for it. - **Cloudflare**: set the A record to *DNS only* (grey cloud). The proxy does not carry mail. - Optional, for a subdomain that only receives mail: `TXT inbound "v=spf1 -all"`. This says the subdomain never sends mail, so nobody can send spoofed mail from it. - Check the records with `nslookup -type=mx inbound.example.com` and `nslookup mail.inbound.example.com`. Changes show up after a few minutes, sometimes hours.

`@` means the root domain itself, so you would use it only if the SMTP server receives mail for `example.com` directly.

For a subdomain setup the names are `inbound` (MX) and `mail.inbound` (A). That is usually the better choice when `example.com` already receives mail elsewhere, because changing the root MX would cut off the existing mailboxes. Either way, on Cloudflare set the A record to *DNS only*.

messages.name: search_docs

[docs/load-balancers.md#the-six-algorithms]
**Static** algorithms follow a fixed rule; **dynamic** ones measure live load per request. Open-source nginx has no sticky cookie or least time (both are NGINX Plus), so pskit builds them: sticky hashes a cookie that holds the first request's id (`hash ... consistent`), and least time runs `balancer_by_lua` with a moving average of each server's response header time. No. Sticky cookies and least time are NGINX Plus features, but pskit builds both on open-source nginx: sticky hashes a cookie holding the first request's id, and least time uses `balancer_by_lua` with a moving average of response header times.

**In the terminal**

```
pskit lb update edge --algorithm sticky_round_robin
```

**In studio**

1. Open **Load balancers**.
2. Set *How it spreads requests* to the sticky option in the form.

Environment: provider=oracle stage=dev mode=auto page=Network map
I set runtime: python3.12 under provider and my target is oracle. Will that work or is it a problem?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/configuration.md#default-runtime]
If you don't pin `provider.runtime`, pskit uses **python3.12** when the target cloud supports it. Otherwise it uses the newest supported version below 3.12: python3.11 on DigitalOcean, IBM and Oracle, python3.10 on Tencent. This is what makes "change only the provider" work. If you *do* pin a runtime the cloud lacks, `pskit validate` reports an error.

It is a problem. Oracle is one of the clouds where pskit falls back below 3.12: its default is **python3.11**. Pinning a version the cloud lacks makes `pskit validate` report an error.

**In code**
The simplest fix is to remove the pin and let pskit choose, or pin the version Oracle has:

```yaml
provider:
  name: oracle
  runtime: python3.11
```

**In the terminal**
1. Confirm the error is gone:

```
pskit validate -p oracle -s dev
```

Leaving `runtime` out is what keeps "change only the provider" working, because each cloud then gets its own best version.

messages.name: search_docs

[docs/cluster.md#how-the-functions-run-in-a-cluster]
* **web** replicas serve your HTTP routes and `invoke()` calls. Adding replicas or servers adds HTTP capacity. * The **main** replica runs on the master with the data volume. It owns everything stateful: schedules run once, not once per replica; built-in queues, topics and buckets live in one place; workflow executions are recorded there; queue, storage and topic triggers run there. * A web replica hands those to main. `submit_queue()`, `put_object()`, workflow starts and `/__pskit/*` admin calls are forwarded to it. Its log lines and invocation counts are sent to main every second, tagged with `replica`, so `pskit logs`, the studio's **Logs** view and `/__pskit/stats` show the whole cluster. * Resources with a driver (Redis, SQS, S3, MinIO, ...) are used directly by every replica, as on one server.

Likely yes. The master runs the main replica with the data volume, and it holds the built-in queues, topics and buckets plus the workflow records. The other servers only run web replicas, which hand that state to main.

```
pskit settings import prod.pskit-settings --dry-run
```

Route lifecycle hooks: if I refactor deploy, which steps must still touch the lb?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/load-balancers.md#create-one-and-put-projects-on-it]
A project names it in `pskit.yml`; every `pskit deploy` updates its route and `pskit remove` drops it: The path prefix is removed before the request reaches your functions (`/shop/orders` arrives as `/orders`) and sent in `X-Forwarded-Prefix: /shop`. `/shop` redirects to `/shop/`. A **cluster** can be attached instead; every deployment on it gets `/<service>/` (or `/<service>-<stage>/` when two stages of a service share the cluster), kept up to date on deploy, remove, join and leave: A project's own `balancer` setting wins over the cluster's route for that deployment. A project whose [placement groups](placement.md) run on several attached clusters gets one route, `/<service>/`, to the servers of all of them; each server passes another group's routes on to it.

Two. `pskit deploy` must update the project's route every time, and `pskit remove` must drop it. For attached clusters, the routes also follow join and leave, so `pskit cluster join` and `pskit cluster leave` count as well.

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#full-vs-code-code-server-in-docker]
1. Studio checks for the Docker CLI and a running daemon. If either is missing, it shows how to install Docker. 2. **Pull & start** pulls the image if it isn't present (the log streams in the panel), then starts `pskit-studio-<id>` with your project mounted at `/home/coder/project`, published on `127.0.0.1` only, and waits until it answers. 3. Adding a new database to the catalog. How does pskit decide between a built-in web UI and a companion one?

By whether the service ships its own UI.

| Has its own UI | Gets a companion |
|---|---|
| RabbitMQ, LavinMQ, MinIO, RustFS, ElasticMQ, NATS monitoring, Mailpit, pskit's S3 and Secrets Manager servers | PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB (Adminer); Redis, Valkey, KeyDB, Dragonfly (Redis Commander); Kafka (Redpanda) and Apache Kafka (Kafka UI); MongoDB (Mongo Express) |

Built-in UIs show their URL and login in *How to use* and *Details*. A companion runs next to the service on a private Docker network, listening on the same interface as the service. Both live in `src/py_serverless_kit/core/onprem_services.py`: add your service to the matching `COMPANIONS` entry and the catalog reports that companion, which the create form shows as its *Also start* switch. Cover a new entry in `tests/core/test_onprem_services.py`.

DigitalOcean API token for a custom resource: where does it go when I write it on the YAML page in studio?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/digitalocean/custom.md#other-digitalocean-services-type-custom]
`custom` is for any service that isn't a bucket, queue, topic, database or cache: Managed MongoDB, Managed OpenSearch, the DigitalOcean API, a third-party API. pskit only passes its connection details to your functions (`external: true` is required). The recipe is always the same: find the **endpoint** and a **password or token** in the control panel, keep the secret in an environment variable, and put the rest in `connection`.

The token goes into an environment variable, never into the file. Everything else (endpoint, user and so on) goes under `connection`.

**In studio**

1. `YAML > Edit raw YAML`
2. Add the resource and the `provider.environment` entry shown below.
3. Click **Apply to draft**, then **Save** in the top bar.

**In code**

```yaml
provider:
  name: digitalocean
  environment:
    DO_API_TOKEN: ${env:DO_API_TOKEN}

resources:
  do-api:
    type: custom
    external: true
    connection:
      token_env: DO_API_TOKEN
```

Create the token in the control panel under **API** > **Tokens** > **Generate New Token**, with scopes as narrow as possible.

Environment: provider=digitalocean stage=dev mode=ask page=Functions
put and get on the R2 binding in my handler, they are async like boto3 or not?

They are awaitables, unlike boto3. Handlers on Cloudflare may be `async`, and `put`, `get`, `delete` and `list` on the binding all return something you `await`.

**In code**

```python
from py_serverless_kit import resource


async def api(event, ctx):
    uploads = resource("uploads")
    bucket = getattr(ctx.raw, uploads["binding"])
    key = "in/" + event.http.path_params["name"]
    await bucket.put(key, event.http.text())
    obj = await bucket.get(key)
    return {"key": key, "size": obj.size}
```

Locally `ctx.raw` is `None`, so stub the binding in tests.

**In the terminal**

```bash
pskit deploy --stage dev
```

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#one-click-services-for-on-premises-functions]
pskit can **create** the queue, stream, bucket, database or cache your on-premises functions use, then add it to `pskit.yml` as a resource and, for queues, streams and buckets, as a trigger. Only the endpoint: boto3 works with RustFS's endpoint like with S3. Read the service by its key and pass its values to the client.

```python
from py_serverless_kit import resource


def list_files(event, ctx):
    store = resource("files")
    return {"store": store}
```

`pskit resources onprem usage files` prints the endpoint and how to connect; hand that endpoint to your boto3 client.

4. Save in the top bar; it goes into `pskit.yml`.

[docs/events.md#schedule]
The handler gets `event.type == "schedule"` and `event.data == input`. pskit converts the portable syntax to each cloud's dialect: A rate that can't be expressed as cron on cron-only clouds (e.g. `7 minutes`) fails validation; use a divisor of 60 minutes or 24 hours. `timezone` is honoured by AWS, GCP and Alibaba (cron form); Azure ignores it with a warning.
Yes, `timezone` is honoured on Alibaba in the cron form, as on AWS and GCP. Without it the schedule runs in UTC.
Where I set schedule in the app?

In the function wizard, when you pick the trigger.

**In studio**

1. `Functions > + Create function`
2. Choose a schedule trigger and set a rate or a cron expression.

```
pskit resources usage cache -p ibm
```

nslookup -type=mx inbound.example.com returns nothing, and we published the MX ten minutes ago. Broken?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/smtp/README.md#dns-records-at-your-domain-provider]
- Most providers want only the part before your root domain in *Name*: `mail.inbound` and `inbound` for `example.com`, or `@` for the root domain itself. `10` is the MX priority; some providers have a separate field for it. - **Cloudflare**: set the A record to *DNS only* (grey cloud). The proxy does not carry mail. - Optional, for a subdomain that only receives mail: `TXT inbound "v=spf1 -all"`. This says the subdomain never sends mail, so nobody can send spoofed mail from it. - Check the records with `nslookup -type=mx inbound.example.com` and `nslookup mail.inbound.example.com`. Changes show up after a few minutes, sometimes hours.

Probably not broken yet. DNS changes show up after a few minutes, sometimes hours, so an empty answer this soon is normal.

**In the terminal**

1. Re-run both checks in a while:

```
nslookup -type=mx inbound.example.com
nslookup mail.inbound.example.com
```

2. If they still come back empty after a few hours, check the *Name* fields at your DNS provider: most providers want only `inbound` and `mail.inbound`, not the full name. Typing `inbound.example.com` there can end up as `inbound.example.com.example.com`.

Shared handlers file + placement: when pskit strips the handlers of other groups from app/handlers.py, is my source file rewritten?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/placement.md#functions-on-several-servers-on-premises]
Per group: one of `server`, `cluster` or `local: true` (the default group may leave it out and use `options.deploy` / `--server` as before), `functions`, and optionally `port` (needed when two groups share a server) and `advertise` (the URL the other groups call, when the server's own address is not reachable).

No, your source is not changed. The stripping happens in each group's bundle only.

- Each server's copy of the shared file keeps just the handlers of its own functions.
- The other handlers, and the imports only they used, are removed from that copy.
- Module-level helpers stay.
- `pskit_host.json` on the server records what was removed, under `stripped`.

Environment: provider=cloudflare stage=dev mode=ask page=Functions
I want to choose the database password myself, not a random one. How?

Put it in an environment variable and pass its name with `--password-env`; without it, a password is generated.

**In the terminal**

1. Set the variable in your shell (the value stays out of pskit.yml).
2. Create the database:

```
pskit resources onprem create orders-db --service postgres --password-env ORDERS_DB_PASSWORD --save
```

**In code**

1. The handler reads the connection from the resource, with the password coming from the environment:

```python
from py_serverless_kit import resource


def orders(event, ctx):
    r = resource("orders-db")
    password = ctx.env[r["password_env"]]
    return {"host": r["host"], "has_password": bool(password)}
```

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#one-click-services-for-on-premises-functions]
pskit can **create** the queue, stream, bucket, database or cache your on-premises functions use, then add it to `pskit.yml` as a resource and, for queues, streams and buckets, as a trigger. It starts the service as a Docker container on this machine or on any server you can reach with SSH. That can be the server your functions run on or a different one. Ask pskit for the connection details; it prints how to reach the Grafana web UI on port 3000 and how to sign in.

**In the terminal**

   ```bash
   pskit resources onprem usage sample-grafana
   ```

2. If the page does not load, check the state with `pskit resources onprem status sample-grafana`.

Sign in as `pskit` with the password pskit stored in your env file.

round_robin seems simple. Is there a catch?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/load-balancers.md#the-six-algorithms]
**Static** algorithms follow a fixed rule; **dynamic** ones measure live load per request. Open-source nginx has no sticky cookie or least time (both are NGINX Plus), so pskit builds them: sticky hashes a cookie that holds the first request's id (`hash ... consistent`), and least time runs `balancer_by_lua` with a moving average of each server's response header time. A server that fails is retried on the next one and rests for 10 s.

It ignores load and is not sticky. It works well when the servers are the same size and the requests cost about the same. For mixed workloads, `least_connections` measures live load instead.

Preflight on AWS, who answer it, my Lambda or API Gateway?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/troubleshooting.md#http]
**CORS errors in the browser** : Add `cors: true` (or a `cors:` mapping) to the route. With `allow_credentials: true` the runtime echoes the request's `Origin` instead of `*`, so list explicit `origins` to restrict who may call. Preflights are answered by the runtime (and by API Gateway on AWS). **405 Method Not Allowed** : The path matched a route but not the method. The `allow` header lists the valid methods. Use `method: ANY` to accept everything.
On AWS, API Gateway answers preflights as well as the runtime, once the route has `cors: true` or a `cors:` mapping. Your handler does not need an OPTIONS branch.

[docs/cluster.md#how-the-functions-run-in-a-cluster]

Environment: provider=onprem stage=dev mode=ask page=YAML
Vertical scaling and horizontal scaling: what do these mean for my database?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#databases-one-server-or-a-primary-with-read-replicas]
- **Single server**: one container on this machine or a server. To scale it up, give that server more CPU and memory (vertical scaling). Nothing else changes. - **Primary + read replicas** (horizontal scaling): the **primary** takes every write, each **read replica** on another server keeps a copy and answers reads, and an optional **load balancer** gives the functions one address that sends writes to the primary and reads to the replicas. Add replicas later as reads grow.

- **Vertical**: one server, made bigger with more CPU and memory. That is how a single server database grows.
- **Horizontal**: more servers. A primary takes the writes and read replicas on other servers answer the reads.
Can I do horizontal later?
With a primary + read replicas you can add replicas later as reads grow.

Redis from a Cloudflare function, options?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/cloudflare/cache.md#workers-kv-type-cache]
Workers KV is Cloudflare's global key-value store: fast reads, eventually consistent writes (changes can take up to a minute to show everywhere). Use it for caches, feature flags and configuration. pskit never creates it: declare it with `external: true` and bind it. Redis clients don't work in Python Workers (no TCP sockets, no third-party packages). For Redis use an HTTP-based Redis service and call it with `from js import fetch`, or deploy that function elsewhere.

| Option | How |
|---|---|
| HTTP-based Redis service | call it with `from js import fetch` |
| Another provider | deploy that function elsewhere, where TCP Redis clients work |
| Workers KV | if a key-value cache is enough |

Direct Redis clients fail in Python Workers: no TCP sockets, no third-party packages.

the notify function can't see PSKIT_RESOURCE_ORDER_EVENTS_ARN, but checkout can. what did I miss?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resources.md#aws-iam]
Each role pskit creates gets a `pskit-resources` policy for the storage, queue and topic resources bound to its functions: If you bring your own role (`iam.role`), pskit can't change it. The plan prints a warning, and granting access is up to you. Narrow the grant by listing `functions:` on the resource.

Most likely the topic has a `functions:` list that names `checkout` only. That list both narrows the `pskit-resources` grant and decides who receives the binding, so add `notify` to it:

```yaml
resources:
  order-events:
    type: topic
    functions:
      - checkout
      - notify
```

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cluster.md#how-the-functions-run-in-a-cluster]
* **web** replicas serve your HTTP routes and `invoke()` calls. Adding replicas or servers adds HTTP capacity. * The **main** replica runs on the master with the data volume. It owns everything stateful: schedules run once, not once per replica; built-in queues, topics and buckets live in one place; workflow executions are recorded there; queue, storage and topic triggers run there. * A web replica hands those to main. `submit_queue()`, `put_object()`, workflow starts and `/__pskit/*` admin calls are forwarded to it. Its log lines and invocation counts are sent to main every second, tagged with `replica`, so `pskit logs`, the studio's **Logs** view and `/__pskit/stats` show the whole cluster. * Resources with a driver (Redis, SQS, S3, MinIO, ...) are used directly by every replica, as on one server.

No need. Schedules run once, not once per replica, because the main replica owns them. Deploy normally.

**In the terminal**

1. Deploy:

   ```
   pskit deploy --cluster prod
   ```
2. Check that the schedule fired once:

   ```
   pskit logs --cluster prod --function nightly -n 50
   ```

X-Forwarded-Prefix value on a /shop route?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/load-balancers.md#create-one-and-put-projects-on-it]
A project names it in `pskit.yml`; every `pskit deploy` updates its route and `pskit remove` drops it: The path prefix is removed before the request reaches your functions (`/shop/orders` arrives as `/orders`) and sent in `X-Forwarded-Prefix: /shop`. `/shop` redirects to `/shop/`. A **cluster** can be attached instead; every deployment on it gets `/<service>/` (or `/<service>-<stage>/` when two stages of a service share the cluster), kept up to date on deploy, remove, join and leave: A project's own `balancer` setting wins over the cluster's route for that deployment. A project whose [placement groups](placement.md) run on several attached clusters gets one route, `/<service>/`, to the servers of all of them; each server passes another group's routes on to it.
`/shop`. The prefix is stripped before the request reaches your functions, so `/shop/orders` arrives as `/orders` with `X-Forwarded-Prefix: /shop`. A bare `/shop` redirects to `/shop/`.

Environment: provider=onprem stage=staging mode=auto page=none
--algorithm choices for cluster load balancer, which exist?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cluster.md#load-balancer-one-url-for-the-whole-cluster-optional]
Add one more saved server **outside** the cluster as its load balancer. pskit runs OpenResty (nginx) there in Docker (container `pskit-lb`, host network) and spreads each deployment's HTTP over the cluster's servers with the algorithm you pick (`--algorithm`: round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin, IP hash, least connections (the default) or least time; `--weight edge1=3` per server; see [load balancers](load-balancers.md#the-six-algorithms)). It works the same way for all three orchestrators. To share one load balancer between clusters and projects by path instead (`http://lb/<service>/`), attach a named one: `pskit lb attach edge --cluster prod` ([load balancers](load-balancers.md)).

Six of them:

1. round robin
2. sticky round robin
3. weighted round robin
4. IP hash
5. least connections (the default)
6. least time.

With the weighted ones you can add `--weight edge1=3` per server.

studio is showing "this machine cannot reach" for my service. what that mean?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/client.md#when-connections-time-out]
`TimeoutError` / `ConnectTimeoutError` / `ECONNREFUSED` from a script almost always mean a firewall: the program can't open a TCP connection to that port. The service is usually fine (`pskit resources onprem status <key>`). Generated direct-client examples use short connect timeouts (about 5 s), so a closed port fails quickly with this explanation in mind instead of hanging. The studio flags it too: *On-prem services → Details* shows when this machine cannot reach a service, and *Call from code* checks the host.

It means the computer running studio cannot open a connection to the service's port, usually because the server's firewall blocks it. The service itself is often fine.

**In studio**

1. Open `Resources > On-prem services > Details` to see which service is flagged.

**In the terminal**

1. Check the service and then tunnel to it:

```
pskit resources onprem status postgres
pskit resources onprem tunnel postgres
```

gpu-box is big and app-1 is small, both behind edge. weighted_round_robin or least_time better?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/load-balancers.md#the-six-algorithms]
**Static** algorithms follow a fixed rule; **dynamic** ones measure live load per request. Open-source nginx has no sticky cookie or least time (both are NGINX Plus), so pskit builds them: sticky hashes a cookie that holds the first request's id (`hash ... consistent`), and least time runs `balancer_by_lua` with a moving average of each server's response header time. A server that fails is retried on the next one and rests for 10 s.

Either can work; they solve it differently.

| | `weighted_round_robin` | `least_time` |
|---|---|---|
| Kind | static | dynamic |
| How | in turn, `weight` times as often | lowest average response time x requests in progress |
| You do | set weights by hand | nothing, it measures |
| Watch out | weights go stale when hardware changes | can favor one fast server until it slows down |

If you know the size ratio and requests cost about the same, use weights. If request cost varies a lot, `least_time` adapts by itself.

Streaming vs Notifications for a contributor example on OCI: which one fits a durable log?

Streaming. Notifications topics fan messages out to subscribers, while Streaming is a durable, partitioned, Kafka-compatible log. In pskit both are bound, not triggered: a topic is a `topic` resource with its OCID, and a stream is a `custom` resource with its OCID and Messages endpoint.

```yaml
resources:
  clicks:
    type: custom
    external: true
    connection:
      ocid: ocid1.stream.oc1.iad.aaaa
      endpoint: https://cell-1.streaming.us-ashburn-1.oci.oraclecloud.com
```

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#one-click-services-for-on-premises-functions]
pskit can **create** the queue, stream, bucket, database or cache your on-premises functions use, then add it to `pskit.yml` as a resource and, for queues, streams and buckets, as a trigger. pskit resources onprem logs sample-rustfs

Environment: provider=onprem stage=dev mode=auto page=none
No Auto Scaling group here, ok. So `cluster join` is how I add servers, and something tells me when I need one?

Exactly. Adding servers is a deliberate `pskit cluster join`, and pskit tells you when it is time:

- `pskit cluster check dev` checks once and sends the alert when the cluster is full; it exits with 3 in that case, so cron or CI can react.
- `pskit cluster watch dev` keeps checking until Ctrl+C.
- `pskit cluster alerts dev` sets who gets told and at which CPU, memory and disk levels.

Then join a saved server:

```
pskit cluster join dev app-2
```

Prod deploy tonight. Is Typesense data backed up by pskit if the box dies?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#one-click-services-for-on-premises-functions]
pskit can **create** the queue, stream, bucket, database or cache your on-premises functions use, then add it to `pskit.yml` as a resource and, for queues, streams and buckets, as a trigger. No. Typesense keeps its data on a persistent volume, so a container restart is fine, but its catalog entry has backup set to no. If the server itself is lost, the index is gone.

Plan for a rebuild instead: keep the source records in your database and re-index from there after you recreate the service.

```
pskit resources onprem create search --service typesense --server db-1
```

code-server inside pskit, this is real VS Code or some small editor?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#full-vs-code-code-server-in-docker]
1. Studio checks for the Docker CLI and a running daemon. If either is missing, it shows how to install Docker. 2. **Pull & start** pulls the image if it isn't present (the log streams in the panel), then starts `pskit-studio-<id>` with your project mounted at `/home/coder/project`, published on `127.0.0.1` only, and waits until it answers. 3. The editor opens inside the studio, with **Open in new tab** and **Stop**. A container that's already running is reused. Stop removes it; your files stay in the project folder.

It is code-server, a full VS Code that runs in Docker on your project and is embedded in the page.

**In studio**

1. Open `Code > Full VS Code`.
2. Press **Pull & start**.
3. Edit; use **Open in new tab** for a bigger window.
When I finish for the day what I do?

Press **Stop**. It removes the container and leaves your files in the project folder.

**In studio**

1. In `Code > Full VS Code`, press **Stop**.

PSKIT_SECRETS_DRIVER=vault, what else I must set for it?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/handlers.md#get_secret-secrets-on-every-provider]
The store comes from environment variables, so the code does not change: `PSKIT_SECRETS_DRIVER` = `vault` (HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao, with `PSKIT_SECRETS_URL` and `_TOKEN`), `aws` (AWS Secrets Manager; Lambda's credentials) or `env` (default: `PSKIT_SECRET_<NAME>`, then `<NAME>`). `store="other"` reads `PSKIT_OTHER_*`. Values are cached for 60 s. On premises a one-click OpenBao, Secrets Manager compatible server or LocalStack writes these variables for you: [resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md](resource-guides/onprem/secrets.md).

`PSKIT_SECRETS_URL` and `PSKIT_SECRETS_TOKEN`, pointing at your HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao server. Values you read are cached for 60 seconds.

**In code**

1. Pass the token through the environment, never as plain text:

```yaml
provider:
  environment:
    PSKIT_SECRETS_DRIVER: vault
    PSKIT_SECRETS_URL: https://vault.example.com
    PSKIT_SECRETS_TOKEN: ${env:VAULT_TOKEN}
```

I create new cluster now. where I choose if master take requests?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cluster.md#load-balancer-one-url-for-the-whole-cluster-optional]
Add one more saved server **outside** the cluster as its load balancer. pskit runs OpenResty (nginx) there in Docker (container `pskit-lb`, host network) and spreads each deployment's HTTP over the cluster's servers with the algorithm you pick (`--algorithm`: round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin, IP hash, least connections (the default) or least time; `--weight edge1=3` per server; see [load balancers](load-balancers.md#the-six-algorithms)). It works the same way for all three orchestrators. To share one load balancer between clusters and projects by path instead (`http://lb/<service>/`), attach a named one: `pskit lb attach edge --cluster prod` ([load balancers](load-balancers.md)).

At create time, with the flag or the switch.

**In the terminal**

```
pskit cluster create prod -o swarm --master app-1 --no-master-serves
```

**In studio**

1. On the `Scaling cluster` page, set the Master serves requests switch in the create form.

You can change it later too, with `pskit cluster set prod --master-serves` or the switch on the cluster page.

Environment: provider=azure stage=prod mode=ask page=YAML
pskit lb algorithms — what does that print, just the names?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/load-balancers.md#the-six-algorithms]
**Static** algorithms follow a fixed rule; **dynamic** ones measure live load per request. Open-source nginx has no sticky cookie or least time (both are NGINX Plus), so pskit builds them: sticky hashes a cookie that holds the first request's id (`hash ... consistent`), and least time runs `balancer_by_lua` with a moving average of each server's response header time. A server that fails is retried on the next one and rests for 10 s.

It prints the six algorithms with their trade-offs, so you can compare before choosing. The **Load balancers** page shows the same, with a small animation of each.

**In the terminal**

```
pskit lb algorithms
```
In the list, what's "static" against "dynamic" again?
Static algorithms follow a fixed rule, for example each server in turn. Dynamic ones measure live load per request, which is why `least_connections` and `least_time` react when one server slows down.

in my bundle i see pskit_manifest.json. what is it for?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/architecture.md#deploy-pipeline]
- **Terraform JSON, not HCL.** The generator builds Python dicts, so there's no quoting or templating to get wrong. User strings are escaped (`${` → `$${`) unless written as `${tf:...}`. - **Reproducible artifacts.** The zip is byte-identical for identical inputs. Unchanged code means an unchanged hash and no redeploy. - **One directory per provider and stage.** Each has its own Terraform workspace and state, so `aws-dev` and `gcp-prod` never interfere. - **Every provider emits a `pskit` output** with the shape `{functions: {name: {id, arn?, url?, base_url?, console?}}, workflows: {...}, endpoint}`. `pskit info` and the dashboard use only this output, which keeps them provider-agnostic.
It is the per-bundle description of every function. At run time `runtime/manifest.py` reads it, so the dispatcher knows which handler belongs to which function.

resources: connection with the real password inline, deploying to huawei. Coming from IAM-auth RDS, is that bad?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/troubleshooting.md#security-notes]
- 500 responses never include exception details unless `PSKIT_DEBUG` is set. - `.env`, Terraform state and `pskit*.yml` are excluded from bundles. `.pskit/` is git-ignored. - `auth: none` routes are public. Embedded workflow orchestrators get a public `POST /workflows/<name>` route unless you set `options.http: false`. - `resources:` connection values are function environment variables: they land in Terraform state and, on premises, in `pskit_host.json`. Pass the *name* of a secret variable instead of the secret ([resources.md](resources.md#secrets)). - On premises, set `admin_token` when the host binds beyond loopback: it guards `/__pskit/*` (queues, invoke, workflows, executions, logs, stats). `pskit dashboard --serve` binds loopback and never sends that token to the browser. - Created AWS buckets block public access. Prefer a least-privilege `iam.statements` over `"*"` resources. - Keep secrets out of YAML: use `${env:...}` in CI or a secret manager via `${tf:...}`. - Report vulnerabilities privately (see `SECURITY.md` in the repository root).

Yes, avoid it. Connection values under `resources:` become function environment variables, so they land in **Terraform state**. Pass the *name* of a secret variable instead, and let the function read the secret at run time.

**In code**

```yaml
resources:
  orders-db:
    type: database
    external: true
    connection:
      host: db-1.example.com
      port: 5432
      password_env: ORDERS_DB_PASSWORD
    functions: [api]
```

Only the variable name `ORDERS_DB_PASSWORD` ends up in the config and state, never the password.

**In the terminal**

1. Validate the change for huawei:

```bash
pskit validate -p huawei -s dev
```

I made orders-db with resources onprem create --save. Now I delete it but the next deploy makes it again?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cli.md#pskit-resources-onprem]
Deleting a deployed resource runs `terraform destroy -target=...`. If it is still in `pskit.yml`, the next deploy creates it again, so remove it from `resources:` (or the trigger) first. Kept resources are deleted from their own small workspace in `.pskit/<provider>-<stage>/kept/`, which is removed when the last one is gone. Credentials are the same as for `pskit deploy`.

That happens because `--save` wrote it into pskit.yml, and a resource that is still listed there is created again by the next deploy. The order matters:

1. Remove `orders-db` from `resources:` in pskit.yml (or remove the trigger that uses it) and save the file.
2. Then delete the deployed resource. pskit runs `terraform destroy -target=...` for it, with the same credentials as `pskit deploy`.
3. Deploy again only after step 1, so nothing brings it back.

Source: [docs/cli.md#pskit-resources-onprem].

**`unresolved variables: env:FOO`** : Set the variable, or give a default: `${env:FOO, fallback}`. **`each event must be a single-key mapping`** : Write `- http: {path: /x}` and `- queue: jobs` as separate list items, not two keys in one item. **`route GET /x is used by both 'a' and 'b'`** : Each `METHOD /path` may belong to one function only (`/x` and `/x/` count as the same path).

Nothing deploys until it is fixed, because a `METHOD /path` may belong to one function only. Give each function its own path, e.g. `POST /run/validate` and `POST /run/charge`, then run `pskit validate` again.

`pskit validate` rejects my `- queue:` line for the SMQ queue. What I do instead?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/alibaba/queue.md#alibaba-cloud-smq-mns-queue-type-queue]
> **No queue trigger on Alibaba Cloud.** pskit's Alibaba provider has no `queue` event: `pskit validate` rejects > `- queue: ...` there. Declare the queue as an external resource and send / receive with the MNS SDK, for example > from a `schedule` function that drains it. Need push delivery? Publish to an MNS **topic** instead and use a > [topic trigger](topic.md).

That rejection is expected: the Alibaba provider has no queue trigger. Keep the queue, but change how the function reaches it.

**In code**

1. Remove the `- queue: ...` event.
2. Declare the queue as an external resource:

```yaml
resources:
  jobs:
    type: queue
    external: true
    name: orders-jobs
```

3. Send and receive with the MNS SDK (`aliyun-mns-sdk`), for example from a `schedule` function that drains the queue.
4. Need push delivery? Publish to an MNS topic and use a topic trigger instead.

**In the terminal**

1. Run the check again after the edit:

```bash
pskit validate
```

Environment: provider=alibaba stage=prod mode=auto page=Setup
SQS leftover and --all-kept after we detached the queues?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/cli.md#pskit-resources-onprem]
Deleting a deployed resource runs `terraform destroy -target=...`. If it is still in `pskit.yml`, the next deploy creates it again, so remove it from `resources:` (or the trigger) first. Kept resources are deleted from their own small workspace in `.pskit/<provider>-<stage>/kept/`, which is removed when the last one is gone. Credentials are the same as for `pskit deploy`.

`--all-kept` is how you delete every bucket, queue and topic left by `pskit remove --keep-resources`. That is the cleanup for queues you detached, closer to deleting leftover SQS queues than to deleting the Lambda functions.

**In the terminal**

1. Remove the entries from `pskit.yml` first, or the next deploy creates them again.
2. Then delete every kept resource.
```
pskit resources delete --all-kept -s prod
```
They are deleted from `.pskit/alibaba-prod/kept/`, and that workspace goes away when the last one is gone. Credentials are the same as `pskit deploy`. [docs/cli.md#pskit-resources-onprem].

Remove server on a row or pskit cluster remove — which one is the destructive one, coming from deleting an ECS cluster?

`pskit cluster remove` is. Removing one server only drains it: its replicas move to the others and the cluster keeps running. Removing the cluster takes the whole thing down, which is why it asks for confirmation first.
For automation, can I skip that confirmation?

Yes, `--yes` skips it:

```
pskit cluster remove prod --yes
```

Use it only in scripts you have tested on a non-production cluster.

Environment: provider=onprem stage=staging mode=ask page=Resources
Rule-printing steps, full list?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/onprem-network.md#network-and-firewall-rules-on-premises]
Which machine must accept **inbound** connections, and which must be allowed **outbound**, at each step: saving servers, deploying, running, clusters, joining servers, load balancers, function groups on several servers, and resources / triggers. Ports in *italics* are defaults you can change. **You do not have to work these out by hand.** Every step prints the rules it just made necessary, with your servers' names and addresses and `ufw` commands: `pskit cluster create`, `pskit cluster join`, `pskit deploy` (one server, function groups or a cluster), `pskit lb create`, `pskit lb attach`, `pskit cluster balancer set`, a project's `balancer` route, and `pskit resources onprem create`.

- `pskit cluster create`
- `pskit cluster join`
- `pskit deploy` (one server, function groups or a cluster)
- `pskit lb create`
- `pskit lb attach`
- `pskit cluster balancer set`
- a project's `balancer` route
- `pskit resources onprem create`

`pskit firewall` aggregates all of them per server.

Ctrl+S not save my pskit.yml when I am on Code page, why?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/studio.md#what-you-can-do]
Every edit goes into an in-memory draft and is validated as you type (the same checks as `pskit validate`, for the provider and stage you pick in the top bar). Problems link to the field they concern. **Save** (Ctrl/Cmd+S) writes `pskit.yml`; undo/redo work across pages. Nothing touches disk until you save, and closing the tab with unsaved changes asks first.

On the Code page Ctrl or Cmd+S does not trigger the pskit.yml save. On every other page it does.

**In studio**

1. Press the Save button in the top bar (title "Save pskit.yml (Ctrl+S)").
2. Or leave the Code page and press Ctrl+S there.

Until you save, your edits stay in the in-memory draft and nothing touches disk.

Private RDS instance and a function deployed with defaults: can it connect at all?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/aws/database.md#networking-first]
An RDS instance lives in a VPC. pskit deploys Lambda functions **outside any VPC** unless you set `functions.<fn>.options.vpc_config` (merged into `aws_lambda_function`). Pick one: A Lambda in a VPC has no internet access and can't reach AWS APIs (SQS, S3, Secrets Manager, ...) unless the subnets have a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints.

No. An RDS instance lives in a VPC, and pskit deploys Lambda functions outside any VPC unless you set `functions.<fn>.options.vpc_config`, so a private instance is unreachable with the defaults. Add `vpc_config` to the functions that need the database, and keep in mind they then lose internet access unless the subnets have a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints.

sshpass not found when our build box runs a password SSH deploy. Which machine needs it, and how do I install it?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#ssh-login-key-agent-or-password]
Password logins go through **sshpass**, so the password never appears on a command line or in the state. Install it on the machine that runs pskit: `sudo apt install sshpass`, `sudo dnf install sshpass`, or `brew install hudochenkov/sshpass/sshpass`. The server must allow `PasswordAuthentication` (many cloud images allow keys only).

The machine that runs pskit needs it, not the target server: password logins go through **sshpass** so the password never appears on a command line or in the state.

**In the terminal**

1. Install it with the package manager you have:

```
sudo apt install sshpass
sudo dnf install sshpass
brew install hudochenkov/sshpass/sshpass
```

2. Run the deploy again with the password still coming from `--ssh-password-env` or a password file.

Environment: provider=onprem stage=prod mode=ask page=Resources
Shell in the container on prod database, each line is separate session?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/resource-guides/onprem/services.md#console-and-terminal]
*Shell in the container* runs any line with `sh -c` inside the service's container. Each line runs on its own (no state between lines), on this machine or over SSH; credentials are hidden in the output. When the image has no client (Dragonfly, NATS, ElasticMQ, RustFS, Memcached), a small helper container joins the service's private network for that command. Servers have the same **Shell** under *Servers*.

Yes, each line runs on its own through `sh -c`, with no state between lines. It works on this machine or over SSH, and credentials are hidden in the output.

**In the terminal**

1. The same as a command, `--shell` gives `sh` instead of the database client:

```
pskit resources onprem console orders-db --shell
```

2. For a real session with history and state, open a terminal instead:

```
pskit resources onprem terminal orders-db --shell
```

oracle send everything like HTTP i read. so my schedule function will think it is http request?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[docs/architecture.md#runtime-flow]
**The `__pskit` envelope.** Payloads that pskit itself produces are wrapped as `{"__pskit": "<schedule|workflow|invoke>", "data": ...}`. These are schedule inputs, workflow task inputs and `invoke()` calls. Because the adapter can recognise the envelope, the handler sees the right `event.type` even on clouds where everything arrives as HTTP (GCP, IBM, DigitalOcean, Cloudflare, Oracle). On those clouds, failures come back as `500 {"errorType", "cause"}` so native workflows can match errors by exception name.

No, it will see a schedule. pskit wraps the payloads it produces, schedule inputs included, as `{"__pskit": "schedule", "data": ...}`. The Oracle adapter recognises that wrapper, so your handler gets `event.type == "schedule"` even though the call arrived over HTTP.

The same trick covers workflow task inputs and `invoke()` calls.
